holistic.reason: Union-friendly, safety-protective design with randomised pilot, audit and paid-time fixes earns approval, but the team-level meal reward and app-friction fixes are modest nudges, and 3-month persistence depends on the app workflow actually being easier rather than on the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: The fixed 20-point crew target ignores baseline headroom, job volume, and case mix, giving crews unequal chances to earn the reward for comparable improvements in practice.

holistic.reason: Unusually careful on union trust, data limits, verification and a safe fallback, but the 30-minute crew reward is modest, the 20-point threshold is demanding, and the proposal is complex, so noticing is moderate and lasting change depends on whether the app fixes make the checklist easier than the paper route.

codex.worst_flaw: The payout gate checks records for digital submissions only, so it can miss both hazards absent from the records and poor-quality checks on paper-fallback jobs.

holistic.reason: Strong on union consultation, safety verification, privacy and fallback handling, but the reward is a modest 30 minutes of team release time with a hard 15-point target, and the copy is low-salience, so employee motivation and post-reward persistence are uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: Learning design is an uncontrolled before/after comparison. It admits it cannot isolate the reward's effect, sets no comparison against plain routing and protected time, and does not handle PR size or complexity mix.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward alongside clearer routing, protected review time, and private feedback, so its before-and-after comparison cannot establish whether the reward adds value.

holistic.reason: It's a well-designed, low-gamification, process-first pilot with private feedback, audits, and a sensible team reward, but the 85% target and credit-per-PR mechanics are somewhat complex, and engagement depends on the routing/protected-time fixes sticking after the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The scale rule can credit the reward for an improvement caused by changes in workload, PR complexity, or growing familiarity with the review process because the pilot lacks a concurrent feedback-only comparison.

claude.worst_flaw: The design is judged only by a before-and-after comparison of three consecutive months. holistic.reason: Unusually well-designed for sceptical engineers (diagnosis first, substantive-review definition, quality sampling with payout pause, no leaderboards, one paid hour reward, honest feasibility framing), but the 8-hour clock plus a weekly 75-minute admin load and a modest reward make the habit unlikely to persist once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group and says itself that a baseline-to-pilot comparison cannot separate the reward's effect from the workflow fixes and private feedback, so the scale decision rests on an uncontrolled before/after result.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a comparable feedback-only condition, so the scale decision cannot establish whether the paid-hour reward improves review turnaround beyond private feedback alone.

holistic.reason: It is well designed, with a diagnosis step, a shared team reward, no individual ranking, quality audits and honest limits on what it can prove, which should suit sceptical engineers. claude.worst_flaw: Credit can only be checked during the sparse monthly observation windows, so the design names the risk that nurses log mainly when observers are present but never tests for it (for example, by comparing kiosk volume inside and outside observed periods), and its learning claim is an uncontrolled before/after on three wards with no comparison ward or seasonal adjustment.

holistic.reason: The safety guardrails, audit-matched credit rule and pause triggers are thoughtful, but a 45-minute-per-ward-per-week reconciliation burden, a delayed credit paid only as a shared ward meal, and a reward tied to kiosk logging rather than hygiene itself make it low-salience and unlikely to persist after the incentive ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The expansion rule can approve wider rollout based on gains the pilot cannot attribute to the meal incentive because it lacks a concurrent group receiving the same kiosk fixes and private feedback without the meal.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design has only a baseline-to-reward comparison, with no plain-feedback or untreated comparison ward and no predefined costs, so it cannot isolate the incremental value of the meal incentive and itself concedes that the baseline only establishes feasibility.

holistic.reason: Safety-first design with independent audit matching, pauses and a diagnosis phase is approvable, but the heavy observer matching burden, a single ward-level meal reward and the one-third/10-point gap rule make it complex and weakly motivating for individual nurses, and with the kiosk fixes retained but no ongoing incentive, durability after the reward window is uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: The design judges success on a before/after comparison with no concurrent control ward, and it says this supports only a feasibility decision. codex.worst_flaw: All three wards introduce the paid-break incentive at the same time, so the scale decision cannot distinguish its effect from growing familiarity with the kiosk or other changes between months.

holistic.reason: Rigorous on safety, verification and anti-gaming, but the reward is a ward-level 20-minute break that is diffuse and small, the sampling-based credit is hard for individual nurses to see, and logging habits driven by a one-month reward are unlikely to persist once it ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward group also gets weekly team progress posts, so the pilot cannot isolate the effect of paid time off queue from the effect of team feedback.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never checks whether a linked article actually helped the next agent or customer (later reuse, handle time, repeat contacts). holistic.reason: Rigorous on measurement, fairness and gaming controls with a sensible diagnose-first step, but the reward is a single paid hour off queue behind a 15-point team threshold, the credit rules are complex for agents to absorb, and the habit has little built-in payoff once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The rollout decision relies on fixed percentage-point thresholds without accounting for ticket mix or uncertainty across teams, so ordinary variation could be mistaken for a durable improvement.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design randomizes 'comparable teams' inside a 60-person org without addressing tiny cluster counts, spillover, case-mix differences or statistical uncertainty, so the 10-point and 5-point scale thresholds cannot be reliably detected.

holistic.reason: Unusually rigorous on diagnosis, credit integrity, quality audit and a reward-free follow-up with comparison group, but the reward (30 minutes of learning time) is modest and the process is heavy for a 60-person team, so agents may barely notice it and the habit may fade once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The in-pilot scale threshold uses a gain over baseline without requiring a gain over the comparison group, so shared workflow fixes could be credited to the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The group-level comparison has too few units to give a reliable result at a 60-person scale, and the design does not address uncertainty, cluster count or programme cost. holistic.reason: Rigorous diagnosis, audit trail, randomized comparison and a retention-based scale test make it safe to approve, but the single paid-hour group reward, heavy credit-lock rules and weekly-huddle visibility are low-salience and unlikely to energize individual agents or sustain habits after rewards end.
